growth_story.headline: Lao PDR's run of 6.1 percent a year on mines, dams and foreign debt slowed to 2.3 percent from 2018, amid debt distress, a falling kip and soaring prices.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Lao PDR grew 3.9 percent a year from 1990 to 2004, as market reforms begun in 1986 took hold, with a setback and hyperinflation after the 1997 Asian crisis. From 2005 to 2017 growth rose to 6.1 percent a year, carried by large investments in mining and hydropower that the World Bank says created few jobs, while many public investments were financed by external debt. The World Bank says this model was already showing strains before 2020, and growth eased from 6.9 percent in 2010 to 5.2 in 2017. The era from 2018 to 2025 averaged 2.3 percent, with a fall of 1.0 percent in 2020 and weak years in 2021 and 2022 as the pandemic, heavy debt and a sharp fall in the kip hit, and recovery has been gradual, with growth of 3.2 percent in 2025, when income per person reached its highest level to date. Over the last decade growth averaged 2.9 percent a year against 6.3 in the decade before, and the IMF still judges public debt unsustainable and expects workers leaving the country and weaker productivity growth to slow growth.

threads.title: Market reforms from 1986
threads.text: From 1986 the government began moving away from central planning under the New Economic Mechanism, freeing prices, unifying exchange rates and opening trade and private enterprise. Income per person grew 3.9 percent a year from 1990 to 2004.

citations.title: The Lao Economy: Capitalizing on Natural Resource Exports (ADB Economics Working Paper No. 330)
citations.quote: In 1986, however, the government began decentralizing control and introducing market-oriented reforms under the New Economic Mechanism (NEM).

threads.title: Asian crisis and hyperinflation
threads.text: After the Asian financial crisis, large budget deficits were financed by printing money and prices ran out of control. Growth of income per person dipped to 2.1 percent in 1998 and recovered to 5.4 percent in 1999.

citations.title: The Lao Economy: Capitalizing on Natural Resource Exports (ADB Economics Working Paper No. 330)
citations.quote: The Lao PDR experienced a period of hyperinflation following the 1997–1999 Asian financial crisis, deriving from monetization of large fiscal deficits.

threads.title: Mining and hydropower boom
threads.text: The fast growth of 2005 to 2017, at 6.1 percent a year, rested on large investments in mines and dams, and exports came to be mostly minerals and electricity. The World Bank notes that these capital-heavy projects created few jobs.

citations.title: Lao PDR 2023 Forging Ahead: Restoring Stability & Boosting Prosperity, Executive Summary (Public Finance Review)

citations.title: The Lao Economy: Capitalizing on Natural Resource Exports (ADB Economics Working Paper No. 330)

threads.title: Debt, a falling kip, inflation
threads.text: Many public investments were financed by external debt, and debt pressures pushed the country into debt distress. From 2021 the kip fell sharply and prices soared. Debt is now falling as a share of the economy, but the IMF still judges it unsustainable.

threads.title: Workers leaving, productivity weak
threads.text: The IMF expects growth to moderate as workers leave for jobs abroad and productivity growth weakens. The World Bank also points to low productivity, skill shortages and gaps in infrastructure as limits on the outlook.

since_last_year.text: Over 2025 tighter policy steadied the kip and slowed inflation, growth was supported by tourism and transport, and income per person grew 3.2 percent, its best year since 2019. Reserves reached a record in March 2026, but an oil price shock in early 2026 pushed fuel prices and inflation back up, and the World Bank expects growth to moderate in 2026.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes a crisis from 2021, with a sharply falling kip, soaring inflation and a large hit to living standards, yet income per person in the data never fell after 2020: it grew 1.1, 1.3 and 2.3 percent in 2021 to 2023 and reached a new peak in 2025. The data measure real output per person, not the loss of purchasing power that the sources describe.
